paper_title: TPHC: Improving Hyper-Connections with Tensor-Parallel Grouped Updates

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Hyper-Connections (HC) expand the residual stream of a Transformer into $N$ parallel streams, and manifold-constrained HC (mHC) stabilizes them at scale. However, mHC benefits little from more than four streams, partly because each sublayer writes a single output to all streams, limiting how differently they can be updated. In this work, we propose TPHC, which integrates tensor-parallel (TP) shards with HC streams to promote greater independence across streams. Specifically, we route a separate mixture of the residual streams to each TP shard and keep the individual shard outputs separate during write-back, so each stream can receive a different mixture of those outputs. This design makes the residual-stream updates more expressive without adding parameters or FLOPs to the attention or FFN sublayers. With native support for stream sharding under TP, TPHC requires only 9% more training time than mHC on an 8B model when both use four streams. Increasing the number of streams from four to sixteen raises its training time by only 19%. On a 1.1B model trained on 100B tokens, TPHC reduces validation loss by 0.7-1.0% and raises average zero-shot accuracy across six commonsense reasoning benchmarks by 0.3-0.7 percentage points relative to mHC at matched stream counts $N\in\{4,8,16\}$. Our code is available at https://github.com/wuyou2002/TPHC.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Hyper-Connections (HC; Zhu et al., 2025a) have recently attracted growing interest as an effective approach to improving the performance of large language models (LLMs). HC expands standard residual connections (He et al., 2016a,b) from single residual path to parallel residual streams, introducing learnable control over inter-layer information flow. Specifically, each sublayer reads *Equal contribution. Corresponding author. 1 learned mixture of the streams and writes its output back to them, while learned matrix mixes the residual streams. Building on HC, ManifoldConstrained Hyper-Connections (mHC; Xie et al., 2026) constrain this residual mixing matrix to be doubly stochastic to stabilize signal propagation across layers. The DeepSeek-V4 series adopts mHC (DeepSeek-AI, 2026a), and DeepSeek-V4.1Flash uses Single-Pass variant designed to enable more efficient kernel fusion (DeepSeek-AI, 2026b). Most HC-family models use =4, since additional streams bring little gain while substantially increasing computational cost. xHC (Zhang et al., 2026) attributes these limited gains to the shared source of stream updates: each stream receives scaled copy of the same sublayer output. Therefore, it proposes temporal feature augmentation (TFA) to address this problem, which derives additional write-back components from causal convolutions of the FFN outputs from nearby preceding tokens. In this work, we explore the possibility of using the partial outputs of tensor-parallel shards as complementary source of write-back diversity. Large models commonly use tensor parallelism (TP; Shoeybi et al., 2019) for training and inference. Consider the computation graph of mHC with TP sharding. TP splits each attention and FFN sublayer across devices by heads or hidden units, so that each shard computes partial output from shared input. An all-reduce aggregates these partial outputs into single output, which mHC then writes to all streams. Thus, the partial outputs already computed by TP are collapsed into the single write-back component. Instead, we propose TPHC (Tensor-Parallel grouped HyperConnections), which treats the shards as groups and preserves their outputs as separate write-back components (Figure 1). In this way, each sublayer contributes separate write-back components rather than one. Horizontal lines are residual streams. (a) In mHC, the sublayer reads one mixture of the streams, and its single output is written to every stream, while Hres mixes all streams densely. (b) In TPHC, the sublayer is split into k=4 groups: group reads its own mixture uj of the streams and returns its own output oj, and Hpost gives each stream its own mixture of the outputs. The illustrated case shows the full update, which writes all streams. The sparse update (3.2) restricts Hpost to the active streams. and Hres l specific inputs as well as outputs. Unlike xHC, our grouped write-back applies to both attention and FFN sublayers by adapting the existing HC read and write mappings to the TP groups, without introducing additional feature-augmentation modules. TPHC increases the training time of mHC by only 78% on 1.1B and 8B models when both use four streams. This grouped design also naturally supports tensor parallelism. Each group resides on separate device, naturally partitioning the group inputs and outputs across devices. The residual streams can also be sharded accordingly, with both read and write operations implemented using reduce-scatter collectives. This reduces the memory cost of the residual streams and makes training models with larger stream counts feasible: at the 8B scale, increasing from 4 to 16 raises the training time of TPHC by only 19%, compared with 59% without sharding. In order to further reduce the cost of the mappings, we adopt the sparse update of xHC (Zhang et al., 2026) with fixed schedule, so each layer writes only of the streams while every sublayer still reads all of them. This reduces the cost of generating the mappings from O(N 3C) to O(kN 2C + k3C). In addition, we initialize each group to read from and write to its own stream. This group-specific initialization breaks the symmetry (Alimaskina et al., 2026) within each sub2 layer and we empirically find it benefical to model performance. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of TPHC. On 1.1B model, TPHC achieves lower training and validation loss than mHC with from 4 to 16. It also improves average zero-shot accuracy on commonsense reasoning tasks by up to 0.7 percentage points over mHC. Notably, TPHC with 8 streams outperforms mHC with 16 streams. Our analysis also suggests that the shared write drives the mHC streams toward common direction, whereas the TPHC streams remain less homogeneous.

Its sparse residual-stream architecture mixes and writes only of the streams, few fixed ones and others chosen per token by learned router, while every sublayer still reads all . It also adds write-back components to each FFN through TFA. Our TPHC retains the dense read and the sparse update of xHC but selects the written streams with fixed schedule and obtains the additional writeback components from the TP partition of each sublayer. Alimaskina et al. (2026) trace the under-use of HC streams to their permutation symmetry at initialization and break it with Learned Stream Scaling (LSS), learnable per-stream scales applied where the residual is expanded into streams. In TPHC, we break this symmetry within each sublayer by initializing each group to read primarily from and write primarily to distinct stream. mHC-lite (Yang and Gao, 2026) builds exactly doubly stochastic matrices without Sinkhorn iterations, and Frac-Connections (Zhu et al., 2025b) split the hidden state into fractions instead of copying it. Other work improves cross-layer information flow by aggregating earlier activations instead of expanding the residual state (Huang et al., 2017; Pagliardini et al., 2024; Xiao et al., 2025; Kimi Team, 2026).

sections.title: 2.2 Tensor Parallelism
sections.content: Megatron-style TP splits each attention sublayer by heads and each FFN by its intermediate dimension across devices (Shoeybi et al., 2019; Narayanan et al., 2021). The first projection is column-parallel: each device computes the queries, keys and values of its heads, or its slice of the FFN units, from the replicated input. The output projection is row-parallel: each device produces partial output in RC, and one all-reduce per sublayer sums them. Sequence parallelism (Korthikanti et al., 2023) rewrites each all-reduce as reduce-scatter and an all-gather. These collectives are major cost, especially in latency-bound inference (Pope et al., 2023). Ladder-Residual (Zhang et al., 2025) reroutes residual connections so that communication overlaps with computation, and SPD (Kim et al., 2025) drops synchronization points after selected attention sublayers. TPHC likewise modifies the architecture around the TP collectives, but instead of rescheduling the all-reduce, it removes the summation of the shard outputs.

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: Compared with mHC, TPHC changes how each sublayer reads from and writes to the streams. Its central component is the grouped hyper-connection, which keeps the outputs of the TP groups separate (3.1). It is complemented by the sparse update (3.2) and an initialization that places each group on its own stream (3.3). We describe the TP implementation, in which both groups and streams are sharded across devices (3.4). Algorithm 1 in Appendix gives the full procedure for one sublayer.

sections.title: Initialization
sections.content: At initialization, the input-dependent component of each mapping is zero, so the mapping is determined solely by its static bias. In mHC, the token embedding is copied to all streams, and each sublayer writes its single output to every stream with the same weight, so the streams remain identical and the model starts as standard Transformer. If TPHC used the same initialization, it would write the sum of the group outputs to every stream, so all groups would read the same input and start as shards of single standard sublayer. In TPHC, we set the bias of Hpre in row j, column sj to +3 and all other entries in that row to 3. For Hpost , we set the diagonal bias entries to +3 and the off-diagonal entries to 3. After applying the sigmoid to Hpre and Sinkhorn normalization to the exponentiated Hres , row of is nearly one-hot at stream sj, and Hpost Hpre and Hres are close to the identity. Thus, group reads primarily from its own active stream sj, and stream sj receives mainly the output oj (Figure 4d). TPHC reduce-scatters the read into the group inputs uj and writes the oj as separate components. The groups receive identical inputs in the first sublayer because all streams start from the same embedding. Their separate writes allow the streams to differ after that sublayer, so the groups can read different inputs in subsequent sublayers. In our ablation, identity write lowers the final training loss relative to dense write at = 8 and = 16 (4.3). Appendix gives the implementation details.

sections.title: 3.4 Tensor-Parallel Implementation
sections.content: Replicated streams. Under standard TP, mHC follows the same strategy as standard Transformer. Every device keeps copy of all streams and performs mapping generation, reading, and writing locally. With TP degree t, one all-reduce per sublayer sums the partial outputs of the shards. In this all-reduce, each device sends 2(t1)C/t elements per token per sublayer, or 1.5C at t=4. TPHC can adopt the same strategy. For t=k, device holds group j, which coincides with its Megatron shard. For t<k, each device holds k/t groups. Each device computes its group inputs locally. Since the group outputs must remain separate, an all-gather replaces the all-reduce. In this all-gather, each device sends (t1)kC/t elements per token per sublayer, or 3C at t=k=4. With replicated streams, every device stores all streams and generates all mappings, so the memory per device grows with . Sharded streams. To reduce per-device memory, we shard the residual streams so that each device holds N/t of them (Figure 2). For mHC (Figure 2a), each sublayer then requires three collectives. The mappings depend on the normalized state of all streams (Eq. (2)), so each device computes partial logits and the RMSNorm statistic from its own streams, and an all-reduce sums them. For the read, each device applies the columns of Hpre that belong to its streams, and since every shard requires the full input u, second all-reduce sums these partial inputs. For the write, each device combines its own streams with its partial output oj, and reduce-scatter sums these contributions and returns the updated streams, so that the residual mixing, the write-back and the all-reduce of standard TP share single collective. At =4, sharding raises the communication of mHC from 1.5C to 4.5C per sublayer (Table 5 in Appendix C), and since mHC writes all streams, its write grows with (13.5C in total at =16). Xl1[Il] + Hpost TPHC shards its streams in the same way (Figure 2b) and differs mainly in the read, where reduce-scatter replaces the all-reduce and leaves uj on device j. Device then computes its group (Eq. (6)), including the output projection, without communication, and the write sums the contributions to Hres Ol with reducescatter, as in mHC. Both reduce-scatters become all-gathers in the backward pass. For =k, device holds stream j. For >k, the streams are placed so that every device holds k/t of the streams written in each layer, and since the fixed streams are written in every layer, the write reduce-scatter delivers each updated stream directly to the device that will hold it next, without separate collective. Across the two reduce-scatters, each device sends total of 2(t1)kC/t elements per token per sublayer, or 6C at t=k=4 for any . The all-reduce for the mappings operates on kN +2k2+1 values per token. Sharding thus raises the communication of TPHC from 3C to 6C, and its overhead relative to mHC shrinks from 3C/1.5C=2 to 6C/4.5C1.3. The remaining 1.5C lies entirely in the read, as the cost of keeping separate outputs, and unlike that of mHC, the communication of TPHC does not grow with .

sections.title: 4.1 Main Results
sections.content: We follow the configuration of TinyLlama (Zhang et al., 2024), Llama model with 1.1B parameters. We train the models from scratch on 100Btoken subset of the SlimPajama (Soboleva et al., 2023) dataset with sequence length 2048 and global batch of 2M tokens. The models are trained with the AdamW optimizer (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019) with β1=0.9 and β2=0.95. We use cosine learning rate schedule with maximum learning rate of 4 104 and warmup of 200 steps. The final learning rate is 4105. We use weight decay of 0.1 and gradient clipping of 1.0. We report the final training loss, averaged over the last 50 steps, and the loss on the full SlimPajama validation set (163M tokens). We also report zero-shot accuracy with the LM Evaluation Harness (Gao et al., 2023) on commonsense reasoning tasks, including HellaSwag (Zellers et al., 2019), OpenBookQA (Mihaylov et al., 2018), WinoGrande (Sakaguchi et al., 2020), ARC-Challenge and ARC-Easy (Clark et al., 2018), and PIQA (Bisk et al., 2020). Table 1 reports the main results. All hyperconnection variants outperform Llama. TPHC achieves the lowest training and validation loss at every , 0.71.0% below mHC and 0.41.7% below mHC-TFA on both, and improves average zero-shot accuracy relative to mHC by 0.30.7 percentage points. TPHC also requires fewer streams to reach lower loss. TPHC4 matches mHC-TFA16, and TPHC8 outperforms both 16-stream baselines. As shown in Figure 3, all methods exhibit their largest gain over Llama early in training, while the gap between TPHC and mHC emerges within the first tenth of training and remains nearly constant.

sections.title: 4.4 Stream Diversity Analysis
sections.content: To examine how the models use their streams, we measure the mean pairwise cosine similarity between streams after each sublayer on SlimPajama validation data (Figure 5a). In mHC4, the streams become increasingly aligned with depth, reaching cosine similarity of 0.985 at the last layer, while their norms remain comparable. The multi-stream residual thus collapses toward single direction, even though all streams remain in use. likely cause is mHCs shared write-back. Hres remains close to the identity in most layers, and the stream norms grow by more than an order of magnitude with depth, so each stream is dominated by its accumulated writes. In mHC, these writes are scalar multiples of the same sublayer outputs, so all streams are weighted sums of the same vectors and differ only in their weights. mHC-TFA4 and TPHC4 both write multiple distinct outputs, the four TFA components of the FFN output and the group outputs, respectively. Both reduce the stream similarity relative to mHC4, and TPHC4 attains the lowest similarity throughout the second half of the network, ending at 0.917 compared with 0.966 for mHC-TFA4. The two differ in the similarity of the write mixtures that different streams receive (Figure 5b). In mHC-TFA4, the attention sublayers still write single output, since TFA augments only the FFN, and even in the FFN sublayers the streams receive similar mixtures (0.79 on average). In TPHC4, whose groups are initialized to write to their own streams, the mixtures remain distinct (0.40 on average) and become similar only in the last layers, where the streams also align.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We propose TPHC, which improves HC by using tensor-parallel sublayer partitions to produce distinct write-back components without increasing the parameters or FLOPs of the attention and FFN sublayers. TPHC achieves lower training and validation loss than mHC and mHC-TFA for {4, 8, 16}, raises the average zero-shot commonsense reasoning accuracy of mHC, and with 8 streams outperforms mHC with 16. We also implement TP with sharded streams for TPHC, keeping the training-time overhead of TPHC4 relative to mHC4 small at the 8B scale and makes TPHC16 affordable. Our analysis further shows that TPHC4 maintains lower inter-stream cosine similarity than mHC4 and mHC-TFA4, consistent with its goal of preserving stream diversity.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Our pretraining experiments are limited to 1.1Bparameter models and 100B tokens, and thus do not cover larger models with more training data. Our work focuses on dense Transformers, where TPHC builds its groups around tensor-parallel partitions. Consequently, the current grouping and communication design cannot be directly transferred to MoE models with expert parallel. We leave the extension of TPHC to MoE models for future work.

sections.title: Ethics Statement
sections.content: This work proposes an architectural modification for language-model pre-training and inherits the risks of the underlying models and training data. It does not introduce new data collection or new capabilities beyond those of standard LLMs. All models are trained on publicly released corpora, SlimPajama (Soboleva et al., 2023) and, for the ablations, MiniPile (Kaddour, 2023), and inherit their biases. SlimPajama is released under the Apache 2.0 license and MiniPile under the MIT license of the Pile, both of which permit research use.

sections.title: A Implementation Details
sections.content: Batched group computation. All per-group projections are stored as tensors with leading group dimension, Rkdoutdin, and applied with single batched matrix multiplication over the groups. The query, key and value projections are fused into one batched GEMM, and so are the SwiGLU gate and up projections. After the projection, the heads of all groups are concatenated so that standard attention kernel (e.g., SDPA) computes attention over all nh heads at once.
